operationalization: Score ink-sac presence and, where volumes are published, relative ink volume across cephalopod orders. Universal discharge is refuted by a cephalopod that lacks an ink sac; the cuttlefish clause needs a quantitative comparison of expelled volume or sac capacity.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts for cephalopods, including ink and defensive traits where they have been compiled

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic frame separating Nautiloidea, incirrate octopods and cirrates so ink-sac absence can be scored by group

obstacles: Nautiluses and some cirrate octopods lack an ink sac, so the universal fails if those groups are in scope.
Copiousness is rarely a comparable numeric field and would have to be compiled from anatomical papers.
rationale: Ink-sac presence is a standard anatomical character and is already enough to test the word 'all'. Relative copiousness in cuttlefish is a second, quantitative claim. SeaLifeBase and the taxonomic literature cover the qualitative character for many species, while a ranked comparison of volume still has to be assembled from papers.

operationalization: Count pereopods, including the chelae, on spiny lobsters (Palinuridae) and brachyuran crabs. The claim is confirmed if both groups have ten and refuted if a species in either group has a different count in normal adults.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: morphological descriptions of lobsters and crabs, including leg and claw counts

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic diagnoses of Palinuridae and Brachyura, which state the decapod pereopod arrangement

obstacles: The last pair is reduced in some crabs and is easy to under-count on a casual inspection.
rationale: The claim is a direct appendage count for two named groups. Decapod diagnoses in WoRMS and the corresponding SeaLifeBase accounts state five pairs of pereopods, claws included. A small team can check the Mediterranean genera Aristotle meant against those diagnoses in days, and a stable deviation would refute the generalization.

operationalization: Measure crusher and cutter chela size in male and female Homarus. The claim is confirmed if every intact animal of both sexes is asymmetric and refuted by a sample of intact animals with equal claws.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts for Homarus describing the crusher and cutter claws

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: compiled natural-history accounts of claw asymmetry in the American and European lobsters

obstacles: The 'never' quantifier needs individual measurements, which sit in papers rather than a trait table.
A lost crusher can regenerate, so symmetry has to be scored on intact animals.
rationale: Crusher-versus-cutter asymmetry in both sexes of Homarus is a standard morphological fact and is described in open species accounts. Those accounts do not contain the individual-level series needed to test whether equal claws ever occur. The sex comparison is feasible; the universal negative is only partly covered.

operationalization: For a taxonomic sample of brachyuran crabs, record whether the right chela is larger. The claim is confirmed if the right side is larger in most individuals and species, and refuted if the bias is absent or left-biased once sampling is balanced.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: crab species accounts that sometimes note heterochely, as a starting catalogue rather than a handedness table

obstacles: Handedness is family-specific, and fiddler crabs and some xanthids do not share one direction.
No open table gives the proportion of right-handed individuals across Brachyura.
rationale: Direction of the larger claw is measurable, and published samples exist for many genera. They are scattered, so 'for the most part' across crabs can be tested only for the studied families. A global proportion would require a new compilation, but existing counts can already support or weaken the generalization inside those families.

operationalization: Code shell chirality (dextral or sinistral) for spiral-shelled gastropods, and the direction of crawling relative to the spire where it is described. One well-documented sinistral species refutes 'all coil to the right'.

candidate_datasets.name: MolluscaBase
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic accounts of gastropods in which dextral or sinistral coiling is part of the species description

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: scope of marine gastropods so coiling records can be attached to a current classification

obstacles: Coiling direction is written into descriptions and is not a single downloadable column.
Aristotle's stromboids are spiral univalves broadly, so the test set is easy to widen past the animals he saw.
rationale: Dextral versus sinistral coiling is a standard binary character, and sinistral species and individuals are already on record. MolluscaBase holds the descriptions, but extracting chirality across 'all' spiral shells is a compilation. The universal claim can be challenged from known exceptions; a complete census cannot be read off one table. The crawling-direction clause is thinner still.

operationalization: Test whether Mediterranean muricids (Bolinus, Hexaplex) and the trumpet shell (Charonia) drill through the shells of prey, and whether the organ used is a proboscis. Confirmed if both groups bore by that organ; refuted if either group does not drill shells.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: diet and feeding notes for muricids and Charonia

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions
candidate_datasets.role: predator-prey records linking muricids to shelled prey

obstacles: Charonia feeds on echinoderms, so the trumpet-shell half may fail even if muricids drill.
Drilling is done by the radula and accessory boring organ, which only partly matches 'proboscis'.
rationale: Shell-boring predation by purple murex is heavily documented, and diet records can separate that habit from Charonia. Interaction databases show who eats whom, while the identity of the boring tool is in anatomical papers. The claim is testable for these named snails, with the trumpet shell and the organ's identity as the parts most likely to fail.

operationalization: The observable pieces are a crustacean body plan and occupancy of an empty shell. 'Intermediate between crustaceans and testaceans' is a rank judgment, and no measurement decides that rank rather than 'crustacean that uses a shell'.
obstacles: Intermediate status is a classificatory conclusion, and shell use does not place the animal between two groups.
rationale: Hermit-crab anatomy and the habit of living in a shell are observable, and Aristotle already states both. Calling the animal intermediate adds a category that no trait comparison can confirm or refute without stipulating what 'intermediate' means. Phylogenetic placement as an anomuran crustacean answers a different question from the one the sentence asks.

operationalization: Mouth position and the location of food can both be recorded. No further observation separates 'the mouth is below because the food is below' from the joint fact that the mouth and the food are both ventral.
obstacles: The final-cause clause restates the anatomy and the diet; it has no extra prediction.
rationale: Oral-side down and grazing on the substrate are measurable and well known for regular sea urchins. The sentence uses those facts as a purpose explanation. Any dataset that shows where the mouth is and what the animal eats is compatible with the bare description and with the 'because', so the explanation is not distinguished from the fact it explains.

operationalization: Count gonads (Aristotle's 'eggs') in regular and irregular echinoids. The claim is confirmed if every sea urchin has five and refuted by species or individuals with four or fewer.

candidate_datasets.name: World Echinoidea Database
candidate_datasets.role: classification of regular and irregular echinoids, the split along which gonad number changes

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts for edible urchins, including reproductive anatomy where compiled

obstacles: Gonad number is in morphological treatments and is not a column in the taxonomic register.
Irregular echinoids reduce or lose the posterior gonad, so the result depends on whether they are in scope.
rationale: Five gonads in regular urchins, and fewer in many irregulars, is a classical anatomical character with an obvious confirming and refuting count. The open registers classify the animals and point at that literature, but they do not themselves tabulate gonad number. A team can still settle the universal for the main orders from published morphology in a few weeks, which is a partial rather than a turnkey test.

operationalization: Record whether sea anemones have a separate anus or void gut contents, and whether nitrogenous waste is released. Absence of an anus can be scored; 'no excretion at all' and 'resembles a plant' need a stipulated meaning before they can fail.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: accounts of actiniarian anatomy and feeding, including the single mouth opening

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic scope of sea anemones so anatomical statements can be attached to Actiniaria

obstacles: Excretion can mean lack of an anus or lack of metabolic waste, and those readings give different verdicts.
The plant comparison is an analogy, not a second measurement.
rationale: Anemones have a blind gastrovascular cavity and release undigested material through the mouth, which is enough to test a narrow reading. 'No excretion at all' also denies metabolic waste, and the plant resemblance does not add a distinct observation. Existing accounts can resolve the anatomical half and leave the stronger wording underdetermined.

operationalization: Bisect insects across a size and taxonomic range and record survival time of the pieces, with body size and chilling as covariates. The claim is confirmed if most insects above a size threshold survive transection and refuted if survival is restricted to a few taxa.
obstacles: Survival after cutting is reported for cockroaches and a few other species, not as a comparative open dataset.
The exceptions for 'cold' and 'minute' animals are too vague to apply without a size and temperature rule.
rationale: Survival after transection is an experimental variable with a clear outcome. Published trials cover a handful of large insects and do not span Insecta, so they can speak only for those species. Testing the stated scope, including the size and cold exceptions, would require new comparative experiments. The existing papers support a restricted-scope test and nothing broader.

operationalization: Treat 'two-winged' as Diptera and score presence of a posterior sting or stinging ovipositor. The claim is refuted by any dipteran with a rear sting and confirmed if the character is absent across the order.

candidate_datasets.name: Integrated Taxonomic Information System
candidate_datasets.role: delimits Diptera so wing number and Hymenoptera, which do sting, are not conflated

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: order-level accounts of dipteran morphology, including the absence of an aculeate sting

obstacles: Sting presence is not a downloaded character for every dipteran family; it has to be read from morphological accounts.
Piercing mouthparts are anterior and must not be counted as a rear sting.
rationale: The contrast between two-winged flies and rear-stinging hymenopterans is a standard morphological distinction. Open taxonomic accounts state it at order level, which is enough to challenge the universal if an exception exists. There is no species-level sting column, so the check is a compilation from diagnoses rather than a direct query, and that keeps the test partial.

operationalization: Score cicadas for a piercing-sucking mouth, for gut contents or feeding site (xylem versus dew), and for liquid excreta. The claim fails if a mouth is present or if the diet is plant sap and honeydew is produced.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: cicada accounts describing mouthparts, xylem feeding and honeydew

candidate_datasets.name: Integrated Taxonomic Information System
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic scope of Cicadidae so the feeding records can be applied to the family

obstacles: Diet and mouthpart structure are in species accounts and entomological papers, not in one trait table.
rationale: Mouthpart type, xylem feeding and copious excretion are standard, measurable characters and are described for many cicadas in open accounts. Those accounts are narrative rather than a downloadable matrix, so a team compiles them. The three clauses of the claim can still be confirmed or refuted from that literature without new fieldwork.

operationalization: A list of receptor systems can be drawn up, but 'special sense' is Aristotle's own partition. Electroreception or magnetoreception counts as a sixth sense only after a rule that his text does not supply, and under his rule several of them fold into touch.
obstacles: Whether a modality is a new special sense or a form of touch is a definitional choice.
The sentence also reports the limits of his experience, which is not a present-day measurement.
rationale: Sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch can be named, and other receptor systems are described in living animals. The claim is that there is no further special sense. That conclusion moves with the definition of 'special sense', so the same organs are compatible with five senses and with more than five. No dataset separates those readings without replacing the claim.

operationalization: Dissect or image the head skin of the European moles (Talpa) and score whether eyes are present, covered, and equipped with lens, retina and optic nerve. The claim fails if the eyes are absent or lack those parts, and holds if covered miniature eyes contain them.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical summaries for Talpa europaea, including the skin-covered eye

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: mammal trait table that places Talpa among the taxa whose morphology can be looked up, though eye structure itself is not a field

obstacles: 'The mole' maps to several Talpa species; the eye description has to be checked species by species.
Eye histology is in papers and museum accounts, not in the mammal life-history tables.
rationale: Covered eyes with the ordinary ocular parts are a concrete anatomical claim, and European moles have been sectioned repeatedly. Open species accounts state the result, while the measurements themselves remain in the anatomical literature. The test is straightforward once the name is fixed as Talpa, and it does not require a new dissection if those descriptions are accepted.

operationalization: Score fishes for behavioral or physiological hearing and olfaction, and for external ear openings and nostrils. The sensory half is confirmed if fishes detect sound and odorants; the 'no visible organs' half fails if nostrils or other external structures are regularly present.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts of sensory biology, nostrils and otoliths for fishes

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape
candidate_datasets.role: ontology-annotated morphological characters for olfactory and otic structures across fishes

obstacles: Hearing and smell have been demonstrated in many species, not in fishes as a whole.
Flight from noise is a behavioral assay and is not the variable stored in the morphology databases.
rationale: Olfaction and hearing in fishes are established by anatomy and experiment, and Phenoscape plus FishBase expose the organs for a large set of taxa. Coverage is still a subset, and the behavioral evidence Aristotle cites, flight from galley noise, is not itself a database field. The claim is testable for well-studied fishes and only partly for 'fishes' as a class.

operationalization: Modern phyla can be listed against cephalopods, crustaceans, testaceans and insects. Membership in his four genera is decided by how he defined the genera, especially the grab-bag 'testaceans', so a phylum that falls outside is an exception he already allowed.
obstacles: The four genera are a conceptual partition, and 'very few exceptions' has no numeric cutoff.
Testaceans already mix molluscs, echinoderms and other shelled animals, so the bins are not independent of the claim.
rationale: Catalogues of animals make it plain that many invertebrates sit outside a narrow reading of the four groups. Aristotle's genera are his own sorting rules, and the sentence already reserves unnamed exceptions. No occurrence or trait table can show that animals 'may be comprehended' in four genera without adopting or rejecting those rules. The claim functions as a classification, not as a trait prediction.

operationalization: Compare sound production in animals that lack lungs (fishes, insects) with possession of a pharynx and lung. A lungless animal that produces a communicated sound challenges the claim only if that sound counts as voice rather than mere noise.

candidate_datasets.name: FishSounds
candidate_datasets.role: inventory of fishes shown to produce sound, almost all of them without lungs

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: links soniferous species to the absence of lungs and to the sound-producing organ

obstacles: Aristotle defines voice as pharyngeal, so swim-bladder grunts can be set aside as mere sound.
The test is circular if voice is defined as whatever a lung and pharynx produce.
rationale: FishSounds documents sound production in more than a thousand fish species, which is a direct challenge if 'voice' means biologically produced sound. Aristotle ties voice to the pharynx by definition and then infers that lungless animals lack it. The dataset can refute the broad reading and cannot touch the definitional one, so discriminating power stays low.

operationalization: Measure gas exchange and ventilatory movements in insects, and score presence of lungs versus tracheae. The claim fails under a gas-exchange definition of breathing and holds under a definition limited to lung ventilation.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: order-level accounts of insect tracheal respiration and the absence of lungs

obstacles: Respiration in his sense is tidal breathing with a lung, so tracheal gas exchange may not count.
Respirometry data are experimental papers, not a comparative open table.
rationale: Insects exchange respiratory gases through a tracheal system, and many ventilate it by abdominal pumping. That is decisive if 'breathe' means gas exchange, and beside the point if it means lung ventilation, which is the contrast he is drawing with voice. Open accounts establish the anatomy; they do not remove the ambiguity in the verb.

operationalization: Vocal repertoires of mammals can be recorded and compared with human conversation. 'Language' versus 'vocal sounds of different kinds' has no decision rule in the claim, so syntax, displacement or turn-taking would be an added definition.
obstacles: Any test has to stipulate what separates converse from complex calls, and that stipulation replaces the claim.
rationale: Mammals produce varied calls, and humans produce language; both halves can be illustrated. The claim that the power of converse is peculiar to man is a boundary he draws inside that material. Studies of ape symbol use or bird syntax become evidence only after a definition of language he does not give, and rival definitions sort the same recordings differently.

operationalization: Compare songs of hand-reared songbirds tutored by another species with their parents' songs, and compare song structure across localities. Learning is supported if tutored songs diverge from the parents and match the tutor; purely innate song would refute that clause. Locality variation is a separate, weaker prediction.

candidate_datasets.name: xeno-canto
candidate_datasets.role: georeferenced song recordings that can test whether notes differ by locality

candidate_datasets.name: Macaulay Library
candidate_datasets.role: archived bird-sound recordings with locality, as a second source for geographic song differences

obstacles: Geographic variation is not the rearing experiment; tutoring results are in papers.
Nightingale and partridge are named alongside small songbirds, and partridge song is a poor fit to oscine learning.
rationale: Cross-fostering and tape-tutoring experiments already show that many oscine songs are modified by what the young bird hears. Open recording archives can test the locality clause directly and cannot replace the rearing trials. The claim is therefore resolvable for well-studied songbirds and only partly for the wider set of 'little birds' he names.

operationalization: Use REM sleep, or filmed sleep vocalization, as a proxy for dreaming in humans, horses, dogs, cattle, sheep and goats. The claim is supported if those taxa show the proxy and weakened if the proxy is absent; barking in sleep would be the direct behavioral criterion for dogs.

candidate_datasets.name: Phylogeny of Sleep
candidate_datasets.role: comparative REM and non-REM durations for mammals, a proxy for the sleep state in which dreams are inferred

obstacles: REM sleep is not dreaming, and the database does not record dream content or sleep-barking.
Behavioral evidence of the sort Aristotle cites is anecdotal rather than tabulated.
rationale: A public mammal sleep database records REM for a subset of species, including some domestic mammals, which is the usual scientific proxy. Dreaming itself is not observed, and dog barking during sleep is not a field in that table. The proxy can show that these animals have the sleep state associated with human dreaming; it cannot confirm that they dream.

operationalization: Apply behavioral or neural sleep criteria to fishes, cephalopods and crustaceans and measure bout length. The claim is confirmed if those groups show sleep and the bouts are short relative to mammals, and refuted if the state is absent in a group.
obstacles: Sleep criteria differ among zebrafish, cuttlefish and a few crabs, and the studies are individual papers.
There is no comparative open database of sleep for these three groups.
rationale: Behavioral quiescence with high arousal threshold, and in cephalopods a REM-like state, has been published for zebrafish, octopus and cuttlefish, and for a few crustaceans. That literature can test a restricted set of species and the 'short duration' clause where bout lengths were measured. It is not a compiled dataset spanning the three groups, so the general claim stays only partly testable.

operationalization: Score sleeping or resting cetaceans for blowhole position relative to the surface and for concurrent respiration. The claim is confirmed if rest occurs with the blowhole emergent and breathing continues, and refuted if sleep is typically fully submerged without surface breaths.

candidate_datasets.name: Phylogeny of Sleep
candidate_datasets.role: marine-mammal sleep records, including unihemispheric sleep and whether animals were in water

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: dive and surface tracks for tagged whales and dolphins that can show prolonged near-surface rest

obstacles: Tag archives rarely code blowhole position as a variable; logging has to be inferred from depth.
Sleep data cover a minority of cetacean species.
rationale: Surface logging and unihemispheric sleep, with breaths at the blowhole, are described for dolphins and several whales. The sleep database and telemetry archives contain the relevant studies and tracks, but blowhole-above-water is usually inferred rather than coded. The posture can be checked for the instrumented species and not for 'all animals with a blow-hole'.

operationalization: Code sexual system (separate sexes, simultaneous hermaphrodite, sequential hermaphrodite) for sessile animals and for testaceans (bivalves, gastropods, urchins, barnacles, ascidians). One dioecious species in either group refutes the universal denial of separate sexes.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproduction sections noting dioecy or hermaphroditism for molluscs, echinoderms and sessile invertebrates

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic scope of the groups Aristotle folds into testaceans and sessile animals

obstacles: Testaceans mix groups with different sexual systems, so the mapping changes the answer.
Sex mode is filled for a subset of species and is often prose rather than a controlled vocabulary.
rationale: Separate sexes versus hermaphroditism is a standard reproductive character, and many bivalves and sea urchins are dioecious while many barnacles and oysters are hermaphrodites. SeaLifeBase records enough of those modes to challenge 'no testacean has two sexes'. Coverage is uneven and the group name is heterogeneous, so the test is decisive for well-documented species and incomplete for the whole class.

operationalization: Score Anguilla for ovaries and testes, for sex, and for eggs or larvae. The claim is refuted if eels have a sex, gonads and a spawning product, and it would stand only if ripe animals and eggs were absent across the life cycle, including the sea.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode, maturity and early-life history of Anguilla anguilla and A. rostrata

candidate_datasets.name: Ocean Biodiversity Information System
candidate_datasets.role: occurrence of leptocephalus larvae, the oceanic young that the river samples miss

obstacles: Silver eels mature at sea, so river catches lack ripe eggs and can mimic the absence Aristotle reports.
rationale: The claim is an empirical negative: eels have no sex and no eggs. FishBase compiles the reproductive biology of the European and American eels, including gonads, spawning and larvae, and OBIS shows the larval stage at sea. That is enough for a standard comparison to refute the universal, once river sampling is separated from the oceanic spawning migration. The analysis is a literature-and-database synthesis of a few weeks.

operationalization: Once each Greek name is mapped, score whether individuals are always ovigerous and whether testicular tissue is absent. The claim is confirmed if the mapped species are functional females or simultaneous hermaphrodites that always carry eggs, and refuted if males without eggs occur.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: sex, hermaphroditism and reproductive mode for candidate identifications such as Serranus and flatfishes

obstacles: Psetta, erythrinus and channe are insecurely identified; only channe is plausibly the comber, Serranus.
Different mappings (flatfish versus serranid versus parrotfish) give opposite sexual systems.
rationale: FishBase can score hermaphroditism and the presence of males for whatever modern species the names are tied to. Serranus, the usual reading of channe, is a simultaneous hermaphrodite and fits 'always with eggs' in a loose way. Psetta is often taken as a flatfish, which is gonochoristic, so the same sentence is true or false depending on the glossary. The data exist and the names do not settle which rows to use.

operationalization: Compare male and female adult mass and longevity within viviparous quadrupeds, and female versus male size within fishes and insects. The claim is confirmed if males are the larger and longer-lived sex in most such mammals (mule aside) and females are larger in most fishes and insects.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote life-history database
candidate_datasets.role: body mass, longevity and reproductive traits for mammals, birds and reptiles

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: maximum length, sometimes by sex, for comparing female and male fishes

obstacles: Sex-specific mass is missing for much of the table, so which sex is larger is often unknown.
Insects, and the mule exception, are outside these two databases.
rationale: Sexual size dimorphism and sex differences in longevity are standard variables, and large compilations exist for amniotes and for fish length. They cover mammals and many fishes well enough to test the two directions of the rule on a subset. Insects and a fully sex-specific mammal sample are not in the same tables, so the claim as a whole, including its stated exceptions, is only partly in reach.

operationalization: Trace life cycles of the insects and internal parasites said to arise from putrefaction and ask whether every individual comes from an egg or parent of the same kind. The claim is refuted if those animals develop from parents, and it would stand if organisms appeared in sterile rotting matter with no propagules.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: life-cycle accounts for insects commonly cited as arising from decay

candidate_datasets.name: WormBase ParaSite
candidate_datasets.role: life-cycle stages of helminths that Aristotle would have placed among animals arising inside other animals

obstacles: The claim names a mode of origin for a miscellaneous set of insects and parasites, so each group needs its own life cycle.
Historical generation experiments are papers, not one dataset of sterile-matter trials.
rationale: The observable content is that some animals appear from rotting material or organ secretions without parents. Documented life cycles of flies, and of gut worms, derive them from eggs and parents, which refutes that reading group by group. The compilations are narrative and genomic-lifecycle records rather than a single experimental table, so the scope 'a number of insects' is only partly covered at once.

operationalization: Compare female and male length or mass within sharks, rays and skates, then within bony fishes. The selachian clause is confirmed if females are larger in most species with sex-specific sizes; the 'most other fishes' clause needs the same comparison beyond chondrichthyans.

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: length and maturity traits for sharks, rays and chimaeras, sometimes separable by the underlying studies

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: maximum and common lengths, including sex-specific values where the source recorded them

obstacles: Many length records are not sex-specific, so female-larger cannot be scored for every species.
The second clause, most other fishes, is much wider than the selachian tables.
rationale: Female-biased size in sharks and rays is a standard life-history pattern and can be checked where sex-specific lengths exist. Sharkipedia and FishBase hold those measurements for a substantial subset and leave many species unscored. Extending the same test to 'most other fishes' drops the coverage further, so the full sentence is only partly resolvable.

operationalization: Score presence of paired claspers at the pelvic fins in male sharks and dogfish, and their absence in females. The claim is confirmed if males of these species have the two appendages and females lack them, and refuted by a species in which males lack them or females have them.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: morphological and reproductive accounts stating that male chondrichthyans bear claspers

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive-trait compilation for sharks and rays, used to confirm the sex difference is general in the group

obstacles: The appendages are claspers and occur in male chondrichthyans generally, so the test should not be limited to a few dogfish.
rationale: Paired claspers are the diagnostic external character of male sharks, rays and chimaeras, and FishBase records them as such. The comparison Aristotle draws, present in the male and absent in the female, is therefore a direct query of existing reproductive morphology. A small team can check it across shark and dogfish families from those accounts without new specimens.

operationalization: Identify the paired milt organs of male fishes and snakes as testes or as something else, and score whether they fill and discharge in the breeding season. The claim fails if those organs are testes; it holds only if sperm is produced by ducts that are not gonads.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive anatomy of male fishes, including paired testes and seasonal milt

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape
candidate_datasets.role: curated presence of testes in fish morphological characters

obstacles: Aristotle's 'ducts' are the elongate testes, so the result depends on whether an elongate gonad counts as a testicle.
Snake gonads are in herpetological anatomy rather than in FishBase.
rationale: Fishes and snakes have paired testes that enlarge and emit milt or semen in season, which matches the seasonal ducts he describes. Open fish-anatomy resources identify those organs as testes. The sentence denies 'testicles' under a narrower picture of a compact gonad, so the same specimens confirm the seasonal paired organs and only refute the claim once his term is aligned with the gonad.

operationalization: Score testis position (internal versus external or scrotal) in birds and in footed oviparous tetrapods. The claim is confirmed if the testes lie in the body cavity in both groups and refuted by a species with external testes.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical accounts of internal testes in birds and reptiles

candidate_datasets.name: The Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic scope of oviparous reptiles whose gonad position is described in the linked literature

obstacles: Gonad position is not a life-history column; it has to be taken from anatomical accounts.
'All ovipara with feet' includes many species that have never been dissected for this character.
rationale: Internal testes are the usual condition in birds and in reptiles and amphibians, and species accounts say so for the common taxa. That is enough to test the claim for birds and for the main reptile groups. There is no matrix that scores every footed egg-layer, so the universal is supported by a broad and still incomplete anatomical sample.

operationalization: Score presence of a urinary bladder in birds, crocodilians, lizards, turtles, frogs and fishes. The claim is refuted if any non-viviparous group other than turtles has a bladder, and it would stand if the bladder were limited to turtles among egg-layers.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: published morphological matrices that code urinary bladder for squamates and other amniotes

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical summaries noting a bladder in frogs and lizards and its absence in birds

obstacles: Bladder presence is coded in some matrices and described in textbooks, not in one complete table.
Aristotle's 'tortoise' has to be kept separate from other reptiles that also store urine.
rationale: Urinary bladder presence is a binary anatomical character. Birds and crocodilians lack one; many lizards, turtles and frogs have one, which is already enough to challenge 'except only the tortoise'. The records are split between morphological matrices and narrative accounts, so a team can test the main groups and cannot download a complete oviparous census.

operationalization: Ask whether female partridges (Alectoris or Perdix) produce fertile eggs after wind-borne exposure, voice or overhead flight, with copulation prevented. The claim is refuted if fertile eggs require sperm transfer and confirmed if fertility occurs with the male only upwind or audible.
obstacles: No open dataset records fertilization without copulation in partridges.
Gamebird breeding results sit in aviculture papers and show that mating or artificial insemination is what precedes fertile eggs.
rationale: The prediction is fertilization at a distance by scent, voice or breath. Managed breeding of partridges and related galliforms treats sperm transfer as necessary, which cuts against the claim, but those results are not assembled as a public dataset of isolation trials. A direct test of the leeward setup is not on the shelf; only a proxy from ordinary breeding practice is.

operationalization: Compare mating posture in octopus, cuttlefish and squid: oral approach, tentacle interlacing, and use of a hectocotylus. The claim is confirmed if all three unite mouth to mouth by interlacing arms, and refuted if any of them mates in a clearly different posture.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive notes for octopus, cuttlefish and squid, including mating where it has been summarized

obstacles: Filmed mating sequences are in papers and archives, not in a posture-coded table.
Hectocotylus transfer does not require the same mouth-to-mouth interlacing in all three groups.
rationale: Mating behavior of the common octopus, cuttlefish and several squids has been filmed and described, so the shared-posture claim can be checked. SeaLifeBase summarizes reproduction and does not code the geometry of the embrace. The three groups do not mate identically, and showing that requires the primary behavioral accounts rather than a single field.

operationalization: For copulating insects, record which sex inserts a genital structure into the other. The claim is confirmed if females generally insert an organ into the male and refuted if the male intromittent organ enters the female in most groups.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: accounts of insect mating that describe male intromission for the major orders

obstacles: Copulatory mechanics are described for scattered taxa, not in one matrix.
A female-above posture is easily mistaken for reversed intromission, which is what has to be separated in the sources.
rationale: Which partner is intromittent is observable, and entomological accounts give it for flies, beetles and others he is likely to have watched. Those accounts are scattered, and a few insects do show unusual coupling, so the generalization can be challenged without being fully tabulated. The test is informative for the orders with good descriptions and thin elsewhere.

operationalization: Compile breeding or spawning month for Mediterranean flying, walking and swimming animals and test whether mating clusters at the winter-to-spring transition. The claim is confirmed by a shared spring mode and weakened if many groups breed at other seasons.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: spawning seasons for Mediterranean and temperate fishes

candidate_datasets.name: eBird
candidate_datasets.role: seasonal breeding codes for birds, as one slice of the 'flying creatures' clause

obstacles: Occurrence month is a weak proxy for mating, and the two databases cover fishes and birds rather than animals in general.
The natural setting is a Mediterranean seasonality that does not extend to the tropics.
rationale: Spring breeding is measurable as a seasonal mode, and fish spawning calendars plus bird breeding records can estimate it for two of the three habits he names. Walking animals and the full Mediterranean fauna are not in those tables. The result can support a spring peak for fishes and birds and cannot underwrite 'animals in general'.

operationalization: If the halcyon is the common kingfisher, compare its laying dates with the winter solstice and with the spring peak of other birds. The claim is refuted if laying falls in spring or summer, and it would hold if clutches were centered on the solstice.

candidate_datasets.name: eBird
candidate_datasets.role: seasonal breeding and occurrence records for Alcedo atthis in the Mediterranean and Europe

obstacles: The halcyon is only usually identified as the common kingfisher; a seabird reading would use different data.
Breeding codes show season and do not pin a clutch to the solstice week.
rationale: Kingfisher laying dates are a standard phenological variable, and eBird breeding activity places Alcedo atthis in the warm season rather than at the winter solstice. That test exists only after the name is fixed, and the archive does not resolve a solstice-timed clutch by itself. Name uncertainty is the main limit on an otherwise straightforward comparison.

operationalization: Use litters or clutches per year for wild mammals, birds and reptiles, and score superfetation in hares separately. The claim is confirmed if most wild species have a single litter or clutch per year, and the hare clause is confirmed if hares can carry overlapping pregnancies.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: litters per year for mammals, including the hare

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote life-history database
candidate_datasets.role: clutches or litters per year for birds, mammals and reptiles

obstacles: The tables cover amniotes, not wild animals at large, and many cells are empty.
Superfetation in hares is a specific reproductive fact beyond the litters-per-year field.
rationale: Litters or clutches per year is the right variable and is already compiled for thousands of amniotes. Those tables can estimate whether a single annual brood is the mode among wild birds and mammals, and they document hare reproduction well enough to inspect the exception. Insects, fishes and unsampled species sit outside the coverage, so the claim's full scope is not in the files.

operationalization: Map pelamys and tunny to Sarda and Thunnus thynnus (or juvenile Thunnus) and compare spawning grounds with the Black Sea. The claim is refuted if either fish has a documented spawning ground outside the Black Sea.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: spawning grounds and distribution for Atlantic bluefin tuna and bonitos

candidate_datasets.name: Ocean Biodiversity Information System
candidate_datasets.role: occurrence records that show the geographic range beyond the Black Sea, as context for the spawning reports

obstacles: Pelamys may be bonito or a young tunny, and the two identifications do not share one spawning map.
OBIS records presence, while spawning locations come from the fisheries biology summarized in FishBase.
rationale: Spawning location is a recorded life-history variable for Atlantic bluefin, which spawns in the Mediterranean and the Gulf of Mexico, and for bonitos, which also spawn outside the Black Sea. FishBase summarizes those grounds. The pelamys name is ambiguous and occurrence is not itself a spawning observation, so the refutation is strong for the tunny once named and weaker for the second fish.

operationalization: For brooding female octopuses, record whether they remain with the eggs, whether feeding trips stop, and whether body condition declines until hatch. The claim fails if brooding females continue to feed at a normal rate or hold condition.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive summaries for Octopus, including brooding where the sources mention it

obstacles: Anorexia and weight loss during brooding are in species papers, not a numeric condition field.
The behavior is described for several species and should not be assumed for every octopus.
rationale: Brooding without feeding, followed by loss of condition, is a measured life-history pattern in Octopus vulgaris and several other species. SeaLifeBase points at the reproductive accounts and does not table condition change. The named behavior can be checked from the primary studies for the common species and is not a ready comparative column.

operationalization: Track gonad index of the edible urchin (Paracentrotus lividus) by month and by lunar phase. The claim is supported if gonads are never absent and peak in spring, autumn, warm periods and at full moon, and it fails if the index is zero in some seasons or shows no lunar peak.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive season notes for Paracentrotus and related edible urchins

obstacles: Monthly gonad-index series and lunar sampling are in papers, not in a public time series.
Aristotle excludes the urchins of the Pyrrhaean Straits, a geographic caveat that modern series may not share.
rationale: Gonad index by season is a standard measurement for Paracentrotus, and published series can test spring and autumn peaks and the claim that gonads are always present. A full-moon effect is much less often measured. SeaLifeBase records the animal and the season in outline, so the seasonal half is compilable and the lunar half is sparse.

operationalization: Compare clutches per year for wild birds with the values for the barn swallow and the Eurasian blackbird. The rule is confirmed if one clutch is the mode, and the exception is confirmed if Hirundo rustica and Turdus merula commonly raise two.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote life-history database
candidate_datasets.role: clutches per year for birds, including swallows and thrushes where a value was compiled

candidate_datasets.name: eBird
candidate_datasets.role: breeding phenology that can show whether swallow and blackbird activity has one or two seasonal peaks

obstacles: Clutches per year are missing for many species, and second broods vary with latitude.
Blackbird and swallow need a geographic scope; Aristotle's birds are eastern Mediterranean.
rationale: Broods per year is a compiled life-history field, and phenology archives add a seasonal check for the two named exceptions. Coverage is incomplete, and a second brood in northern Europe does not decide the Mediterranean populations he observed. The rule and the two exceptions can be examined for well-documented species and not for wild birds as a class.

operationalization: Rank body mass, and wing or body length if needed, for Columba palumbus, Columba oenas, Columba livia and Streptopelia turtur. The claim is confirmed if mass decreases in that order, with the stock dove only slightly above the rock pigeon, and refuted by any other order.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: species-level body mass and linear measurements for all birds, including these four columbids

obstacles: Mass is a proxy for the size ranking; a length ranking could in principle differ, though both are in the same table.
The common pigeon is read here as Columba livia, including its wild and feral forms.
rationale: AVONET provides comparable body mass and morphological measurements for the wood pigeon, stock dove, rock pigeon and turtle dove. The claimed order is a direct sort of those values. A small team can run it in a day, and a reversal of any adjacent pair would refute the ranking.

operationalization: Compare fertility of the first ejaculates, or size of the first eggs and offspring, with later ones in humans, livestock and birds. The claim is confirmed if the earliest products are infertile or yield smaller young, and refuted if first and later products match.
obstacles: Parity-specific fertility and first-clutch size are in livestock, poultry and clinical papers, not a cross-taxon table.
The claim covers 'all animals', far beyond the species with a first-versus-later comparison.
rationale: First-egg size in poultry and age-related semen quality in mammals are measured variables, and published series exist for chickens, some livestock and humans. They are not gathered into an open comparative file, and they do not span animals in general. A subset of the claim can be inspected from that literature; the universal cannot.

operationalization: Estimate age at spermarche and age at which males can sire a pregnancy. The claim is confirmed if semen appears near fourteen and effective fertility begins near twenty-one, and it is refuted if fertility begins with puberty rather than at twenty-one.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: age at sexual maturity for Homo sapiens, a single maturity age rather than two thresholds

candidate_datasets.name: Human Fertility Database
candidate_datasets.role: age-specific fertility, used to see whether male or couple fertility is delayed until about twenty-one

obstacles: Open tables give one maturity age or births by age, not a separate age of first semen versus first fertile capacity.
Paternal age at birth is thinner in the public fertility tables than maternal age.
rationale: Spermarche near the early teens is a published developmental statistic, and AnAge records a single age at sexual maturity for humans close to that range. The second threshold, generative capacity only at about twenty-one, is a different claim and is not a field in these databases. Age-specific fertility can pressure that second number without isolating male spermarche.

operationalization: Compare fundamental frequency of calls or speech by sex and by age in humans, deer, dogs and horses. The claim is confirmed if females and juveniles have higher pitch in most of these species, and refuted if the pattern is absent or reversed in most of them.
obstacles: No open cross-species table of fundamental frequency by sex and age exists for the mammals named.
Published spectra are species-by-species papers and use different call types.
rationale: Pitch by sex and age is a clear acoustic measurement, and human voice data plus scattered mammal studies can address pieces of the rule. They are not harmonized into a dataset covering deer, dogs, horses and humans together. A team can assemble a partial comparison from papers over months, which is short of a ready test of the general rule.

operationalization: Measure fundamental frequency of cow, bull and calf calls under the same recording protocol. The claim is confirmed if cows are lower than bulls and calves lower than adults, and refuted if bulls are lower than cows or adults lower than calves.
obstacles: Cattle-call spectra exist in a few bioacoustic papers and are not compiled as paired sex and age samples.
Call type (contact, distress, roar) changes pitch and has to be matched before sexes are compared.
rationale: The comparison is a simple acoustic contrast and would cleanly support or refute the exception Aristotle states for cattle. Existing recordings are few, unmatched across call types, and not deposited as an analysis-ready table. They allow a preliminary look and do not yet decide the claim.

operationalization: Compare voice pitch and other sex characters before and after castration in males, against intact males and females. The claim is supported if gelded males shift toward female values, and refuted if castration leaves those characters unchanged.
obstacles: Castration effects on voice and plumage or antlers are in veterinary and endocrine papers, not a comparative dataset.
The species he has in mind (man, deer, birds) need to be analyzed separately because the traits differ.
rationale: The effect of removing the testes on voice and secondary characters is experimentally tractable and has been measured in humans, deer, capons and other domestic animals. Those results can test the mechanism for several species. They are not in one open table, so the cross-species claim is only partly assembled.

operationalization: Compare published gestation lengths for the domestic dog with the interval 60 to 63 days, and, where litter-level data exist, test whether gestations under 60 days fail. The duration claim fails if the typical range lies outside that window.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length for Canis lupus familiaris

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: an independent gestation-length value for the dog or wolf

obstacles: Both databases report a species-level duration, not the claim that litters born before 60 days die.
rationale: Gestation length of the dog is a standard field in AnAge and PanTHERIA, and the stated window of 60 to 63 days can be compared with those values directly. The further claim about non-survival of shorter litters is not in the tables and remains a veterinary detail. The central duration is resolvable with the life-history databases now.

operationalization: Compare typical adult lifespan of stallions and mares with 35 and a little over 40 years, keeping maximum records separate. The claim is confirmed if typical male and female longevities fall near those figures, with mares living longer, and refuted if typical lifespans or the sex order differ.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: maximum longevity and, where recorded, sex of the record for Equus caballus

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: maximum longevity for the horse as a second compiled estimate

obstacles: The open fields are maximum longevity, while the claim is a typical lifespan.
Sex-specific typical ages are not separate columns, and record ages exceed both stated figures.
rationale: AnAge and PanTHERIA give horse longevity, so a numerical comparison is immediate. They record maxima and exceptional ages, whereas Aristotle states a usual life of about 35 years for stallions and a little over 40 for mares. The sex difference in typical lifespan is therefore only partly addressed by the same sources, and a maximum above 40 does not by itself refute a statement about the usual life.

operationalization: Use age-specific fertility to find the ages at which male and female fertility become rare, and compare them with about 65 and about 45, and with the outer limits of 70 and 50. The claim fails if the ages at which fertility effectively ends lie well away from those figures.

candidate_datasets.name: Human Fertility Database
candidate_datasets.role: age-specific fertility rates that show until what age women bear children

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive lifespan context for Homo sapiens, complementary to the fertility schedule

obstacles: The Human Fertility Database measures births by maternal age; paternal age is much less complete.
Modern fertility is shaped by contraception and is a biased proxy for biological capacity.
rationale: Female age-specific fertility is a public, analysis-ready series and can test the claim that conception becomes rare around forty-five and exceptional by fifty. Male fertility to sixty-five or seventy is not in the same table at comparable coverage. Social control of fertility also separates observed births from biological capacity, so the female half is testable and the male half and the biological reading remain partial.

operationalization: Compare gestation length and litter size of Camelus dromedarius with twelve months and one young. The claim is confirmed if gestation is about twelve months and twinning is absent or exceptional, and refuted if either value is substantially different.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length and litter size for the dromedary

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: independent gestation length and litter size for camels

obstacles: Published gestations cluster near twelve to thirteen months, so 'twelve' is a rounded target rather than an exact day count.
rationale: Gestation length and litter size of the dromedary are both fields in AnAge and PanTHERIA. Either database can confirm or refute a twelve-month pregnancy and single young. The analysis is a direct lookup, with the only subtlety being that reported means sit slightly above twelve months.

operationalization: Compare gestation and litter size of Elephas maximus and Loxodonta africana with two years and one calf. The claim is confirmed if gestation is about twenty-four months and twin births are absent or rare, and refuted if gestation or the usual litter size differs.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length and litter size for both living elephant species

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: a second compiled gestation and litter size for elephants

obstacles: The two living species differ by weeks, and 'two years' has to be scored against means near twenty-two months.
Rare twin births mean 'only one' is a rule about the usual litter, not a strict impossibility.
rationale: Elephant gestation and litter size are standard entries in the mammal life-history databases. Those values can confirm a single calf and can show whether 'two years' matches the measured pregnancy or overshoots it. The comparison is immediate and decides the claim as a quantitative generalization, with species differences and rare twins as stated caveats rather than missing data.

operationalization: Estimate lifespan of Bolinus brandaris and Hexaplex trunculus and test whether spiral checks are annual. The claim is confirmed if typical life is about six years and each check matches one year, and refuted if lifespan or the check interval differs.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: longevity and growth notes for the purple murex species, where a value has been entered

candidate_datasets.name: MolluscaBase
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic identity of the Mediterranean purple murex so growth studies can be matched to species

obstacles: Longevity entries are sparse, and annual shell checks are a sclerochronology result in papers.
Bolinus and Hexaplex need not share one lifespan.
rationale: Lifespan and the meaning of shell increments are measurable, and growth studies exist for the Mediterranean muricids. SeaLifeBase may carry a longevity figure and does not encode whether each spiral interval is one year. Both halves of the sentence can be pursued in the primary literature for these species and are not in a ready comparative file.

operationalization: Record whether Pinna nobilis houses a shrimp or pea crab, and whether experimental removal raises mortality. The association is confirmed by co-occurrence; the claim that the mussel soon dies without the guest requires a removal result.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions
candidate_datasets.role: commensal and host records linking Pinna with pontoniine shrimps and pea crabs

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: species account of Pinna nobilis and notes on its associated crustaceans

obstacles: Interaction records show co-occurrence, not death after removal.
The guest is sometimes a shrimp and sometimes a crab, so 'the' pinna-guard is not one species.
rationale: The housing of a small crustacean in Pinna is a documented association and can be read from interaction compilations. The further claim that the mussel dies soon after losing that companion is a causal mortality statement and is not what those records contain. Existing data can test the partnership and leave the death clause weakly constrained.

operationalization: Test two predictions: that bivalves, gastropods, barnacles and ascidians arise without parents from mud, and that oysters, cockles and limpets sort onto slime, sand and rock. Life cycles with larvae or eggs refute spontaneous generation; habitat frequencies test the substrate sorting.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: larval development and habitat notes for oysters, cockles, mussels, limpets and barnacles

candidate_datasets.name: Ocean Biodiversity Information System
candidate_datasets.role: occurrences with substrate or habitat context for the same groups

obstacles: Habitat fields are coarse, so slime versus sand versus rock hollows is only partly captured.
Spontaneous generation is refuted by life cycles that are described species by species.
rationale: Larval life cycles of oysters, cockles and limpets are on record and contradict an origin from mud without parents. Substrate preferences are a separate, genuine pattern and can be compared with occurrence data where habitat was recorded. The mechanistic half is decidable from existing life histories, and the habitat half is only as sharp as the substrate fields.

operationalization: Measure egg diameter at laying and during incubation for a lobster or crayfish, a cephalopod and an oviparous fish. The claim is confirmed if diameter increases after laying in each group and refuted if size is fixed at deposition.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: egg-size records for oviparous fishes, a baseline rather than a swelling time series

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: egg and early-development notes for crustaceans and cephalopods

obstacles: Post-laying swelling is measured in species studies and is not a comparative field.
Water uptake at fertilization has to be separated from later embryonic growth.
rationale: An increase in egg size after laying is a simple measurement, and it has been reported for fish eggs that harden by water uptake and for some cephalopod and crustacean eggs. The life-history databases store a single egg size, not the before-and-after contrast. The claim is testable from those studies for particular species and is not a column one can average across the three groups.

operationalization: Compare maximum or typical lifespan of squid, cuttlefish and octopus with one year. The claim is confirmed if almost all species die within a year and refuted if a substantial set lives longer.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: longevity entries for squids, cuttlefishes and octopuses

obstacles: Lifespan is filled for a minority of species.
Some octopuses, and nautiluses if they are admitted, live well beyond a year, so scope decisions matter.
rationale: SeaLifeBase contains longevity for a number of cephalopods, which is the right variable for a one-year limit. Many common octopuses and squids are short-lived, and several documented lifespans exceed a year, so the 'few exceptions' clause can be inspected where a number exists. Missing entries for most species keep the test partial.

operationalization: Ask whether the adult insect is formed from the whole larval body or from imaginal discs while most larval tissue is broken down, and whether any butterflies lay a hard egg rather than a grub-producing egg. The 'whole grub' clause fails if the adult arises from discrete primordia.

candidate_datasets.name: FlyBase
candidate_datasets.role: developmental records of imaginal discs in Drosophila, the best-tabulated case of adult tissue arising from parts of the larva

obstacles: The detailed map of imaginal discs is for Drosophila, not for insects generally.
What counts as 'a portion' of the grub versus the whole grub is a histological judgment.
rationale: FlyBase documents that the adult fly is assembled from imaginal discs while much of the larva is histolyzed, which is a direct contrast with 'the grub entire becomes the animal'. That is one model species. The exception for a butterfly that lays a hard egg, and the same contrast in bees and beetles, remain in the broader developmental literature rather than in that database.

operationalization: Map the three worms to tapeworm, Ascaris and pinworm and score whether adults produce eggs or larvae that become the next generation. The claim is refuted if any of them reproduces, and the melon-seed clause can be compared with tapeworm proglottids.

candidate_datasets.name: WormBase ParaSite
candidate_datasets.role: lifecycle-stage records for Ascaris, cestodes and pinworms showing egg, larva and adult generations

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions
candidate_datasets.role: host records for these worms in humans, consistent with transmission between hosts

obstacles: The three Greek kinds are approximate matches to tapeworm, roundworm and pinworm.
Lifecycle stages in a genome resource are not a demographic demonstration of fertility, though they record the successive generations.
rationale: Whether intestinal worms produce offspring is decided by their life cycles, which include eggs and larvae for all three modern counterparts. WormBase ParaSite organizes those stages, and interaction records place the worms in human hosts across generations. The name match is approximate and the databases are not fertility trials, so the refutation is strong in substance and still one step removed from a purpose-built table.

operationalization: Score feeding and defecation in larvae and in pupae of butterflies, bees and wasps. The claim is confirmed if caterpillars and grubs do both and pupae do neither, and refuted if pupae feed or regularly void gut contents.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: life-cycle accounts of feeding larvae and non-feeding pupae in Lepidoptera and Hymenoptera

obstacles: The pattern is in natural-history accounts rather than a trait matrix of gut activity.
Meconium voided at eclosion can be mistaken for pupal excretion if the stage is not timed carefully.
rationale: Feeding and defecation by stage are observable, and accounts of butterflies, bees and wasps describe feeding larvae and quiescent pupae. That literature can test the claim for the main holometabolous groups he names. It is not a downloaded character, and a few edge cases around emergence have to be kept separate from pupal life.

operationalization: Separate two readings: development rate depends on heat, and generation is caused by the sun or the wind rather than by parents. Degree-day series test the first; a life cycle from eggs tests the second. Only the second discriminates the claim from ordinary reproduction in warm weather.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: parental life cycles of insects that pass through a grub, the observation that distinguishes parental generation from sun or wind

obstacles: Temperature speeds development and does not show that the sun or the wind is the cause of generation.
Wind as a generative cause has no separate measurement.
rationale: Insect development is temperature-dependent, and that fact is compatible with ordinary egg-laying in warm weather. The sentence says generation is due primarily to the sun or the wind. Life-cycle accounts that derive grubs from eggs refute that causal claim for the species they cover, while no dataset isolates wind as a cause. The test works only on the parental-origin reading and only for compiled life cycles.

operationalization: Search copper-smelting fires for a winged insect, larger than a bluebottle, that lives in the fire and dies when removed. The claim is confirmed by a sustained population in the fire and refuted by monitored furnaces in which no such animal occurs.
obstacles: Faunal lists of Cyprus do not encode a habitat of 'inside the fire', so absence from those lists is not the test.
Ancient smelting heaps are not a sampled environment in any open occurrence dataset.
rationale: The report is a concrete natural-history claim: a winged animal is generated in Cypriot copper fires and depends on the fire. No public dataset records animals living in smelting furnaces, and species catalogues cannot substitute for that microhabitat. A test would require new observation at operating or reconstructed furnaces. Until then the claim is unresolvable with existing data.

operationalization: Identify the wasp, then score whether females kill spiders, seal them in a mud-closed hole, and develop their young there. The claim is confirmed for pompilids or mud-daubers if that sequence holds and weakened if the animals are ichneumonid parasitoids with a different habit.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions
candidate_datasets.role: wasp-spider predation and provisioning records

candidate_datasets.name: WaspWeb
candidate_datasets.role: biology pages for spider-hunting wasps and mud-daubers, used to fix the Greek name

obstacles: 'Ichneumon' in modern taxonomy is a parasitoid family, while the described habit matches pompilids or mud-daubers.
Mud-sealing and the kill are behavioral details only partly captured by interaction records.
rationale: Spider-provisioning and mud closures are well described for pompilid wasps and for Sceliphron mud-daubers, and interaction databases record wasp-spider links. Aristotle's name points at ichneumons, whose modern members mostly parasitize other hosts. Once the animal is identified from the behavior, the sequence can be checked; the name itself makes the test ambiguous.

operationalization: Trace the carbon source of beeswax and of honey in Apis mellifera, and test whether honey matches floral nectar or atmospheric dew. Wax synthesized from metabolized sugars, and honey made from nectar, refute the split he states; honey chemically identical to dew would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions
candidate_datasets.role: flower-visitation records for Apis, a proxy for a floral source of nectar and not a chemical assay of honey

obstacles: Nectar-to-honey conversion and wax-gland synthesis are in apicultural chemistry papers, not one open table.
Visitation records cannot by themselves show that honey is collected dew.
rationale: The two clauses make opposite claims about origins: wax is made from flowers, honey is gathered from the air. Chemical and behavioral studies of Apis mellifera identify nectar as the honey source and wax as a glandular secretion fed by that sugar. Those results are published in detail and are not deposited as a single analysis-ready dataset, so a team synthesizes them rather than downloading a column. The discriminating evidence exists and still has to be compiled.

operationalization: Estimate lifespan separately for workers, queens and colonies and compare each with six years, or seven at most. The claim is confirmed for whichever bearer is intended if that lifespan is usually six and at most seven, and the test is blocked while the bearer is unspecified.
obstacles: Worker, queen and colony lifespans differ by orders of magnitude, and the text does not say which is meant.
Queen and colony survival figures are in apicultural reports rather than a life-history database of the AnAge kind.
rationale: A numerical lifespan is easy to test once the individual is fixed. Workers live weeks to months, queens often a few years, and colonies can persist longer, so the same figure of six or seven years is plausible for one reading and false for another. No open longevity table removes that ambiguity. The data can test each reading and cannot decide which reading the sentence asserts.

operationalization: Record whether scorpion young kill the mother after leaving her back, and whether spiderlings kill the mother, by species. The claim is confirmed if matriphagy or matricide follows hatching in scorpions and in spiders generally, and refuted if the young disperse without killing the parent.

candidate_datasets.name: World Spider Trait database
candidate_datasets.role: curated spider traits, including behavioral records such as maternal care and matriphagy where contributors have entered them

candidate_datasets.name: World Spider Catalog
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic frame for the spider species in which offspring consume the mother

obstacles: Matriphagy is known in some spiders and is not the spider life cycle.
Scorpion broods ride on the mother; killing her is not a tabulated outcome and is not the usual account.
rationale: Offspring killing the parent is a behavioral event, and it is documented for particular spiders such as Stegodyphus. Spider trait compilations can hold that behavior when it has been entered, and they do not show it as general. Scorpion maternal care is described in the opposite direction, from papers rather than from the spider databases. The spider half is partly testable and the scorpion half is a separate, thinly tabulated claim.

operationalization: For Mediterranean acridids, record oviposition date and whether adults die after laying, males included. The claim is confirmed if eggs are laid at the end of summer and both sexes then die, and refuted if adults overwinter or lay earlier and survive.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: life-cycle summaries for grasshoppers, including season of oviposition and annual adult death where described

obstacles: 'Grasshopper' covers many species, only some of which are strictly semelparous annuals.
Phenology is regional, and a northern European calendar need not match Greece.
rationale: End-of-summer oviposition followed by adult death is a recognizable annual life cycle and is described for many temperate grasshoppers. The accounts are species-level natural history, not a phenology table for the Greek fauna, and some species overwinter as adults or lay over a longer season. The pattern can be checked for familiar species and not confirmed as the grasshopper life cycle.

operationalization: Score tymbal presence and calling by sex in cicadas. The claim is confirmed if only males call and females are silent, and refuted if females produce the song or males of a singing species are silent.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: cicada accounts stating that males sing and females do not

obstacles: Sex of the singer is in morphological accounts and is not a downloaded character for every cicada species.
Some females produce soft sounds that have to be distinguished from the male song.
rationale: Male-only song, produced by timbals, is a standard sex character in cicadas and is stated in open family accounts. That is enough to test the claim for the well-known species and for the family-level generalization. There is no species-by-sex song matrix, so confirming it for both of Aristotle's size classes still means reading the morphological literature.

operationalization: Follow eggs ('nits') of lice, fleas and bedbugs to the next stage. The claim is refuted if nits hatch into nymphs that become reproductive adults, and it would stand if the eggs produced nothing further.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: life cycles of Pediculus, Pulex and Cimex from egg through nymph to adult

obstacles: Life cycles are narrative species accounts rather than a stage-structured dataset.
Bedbug, flea and louse eggs are all called nits in the claim and have to be matched separately.
rationale: The life cycles of human lice, fleas and bedbugs are standard and state that the egg hatches into a nymph which becomes an adult. Open species accounts carry that sequence. They are not a single demographic table, but they are sufficient to confirm or refute the claim that the nit generates nothing, for these three parasites, without new rearing.

operationalization: Search host-parasite records for lice and ticks on Equus asinus, and compare with records on other mammals and birds. The donkey exception is refuted by a credible louse or tick record; the universal infestation of all other hairy and feathered animals needs a much wider host survey.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions
candidate_datasets.role: host-parasite records for lice and ticks on donkeys and other mammals and birds

obstacles: A positive record can refute the donkey exception, while 'all other animals are infested' is far broader than the interaction tables.
Veterinary records and wildlife records are unevenly digitized, so absence is weak evidence.
rationale: GloBI aggregates parasite-host interactions, which is the right structure for lice and ticks on Equus asinus. A documented infestation refutes the claimed exemption. The same tables cannot show that every other bird and mammal is infested, because most hosts have never been surveyed into the database. The exception is testable and the universal is not.

operationalization: Follow Blastophaga psenes from caprifigs into the ostiole of cultivated Ficus carica and test whether fruit drop increases when wasps are excluded. The claim is confirmed if wasps reared in wild figs enter edible figs and retention depends on that entry, and refuted if exclusion does not increase drop.

candidate_datasets.name: FigWeb
candidate_datasets.role: biology of the fig-wasp mutualism, including Blastophaga psenes, caprifigs and the cultivated fig

obstacles: Fruit retention is an agricultural outcome of pollination, and the trials that measure drop are summarized rather than stored as a raw table on the site.
rationale: FigWeb documents the caprifig cycle of Blastophaga psenes and the entry of the wasps into edible figs, which is the natural-history core of the claim. Exclusion experiments showing that unpollinated figs drop are part of the same published system the site organizes. A team can compare the sentence with that body of evidence in a short review; the only gap is that the drop counts themselves are in the agronomic papers rather than in a fresh download.

operationalization: Code reproductive mode and litter size for vipers and for other snakes. Viviparity with retained eggs confirms the viper clause; oviparity in vipers, or viviparity widespread in other snakes, challenges the contrast. Litter size near twenty and birth within one day are separate numeric checks.

candidate_datasets.name: The Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode and litter or clutch size for vipers and other snakes

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote life-history database
candidate_datasets.role: litter size and related reproductive traits for snakes, as a numeric check on 'about twenty'

obstacles: 'The viper' covers several species whose litter sizes are not all near twenty.
Many boas, sea snakes and some colubrids are also viviparous, so 'other serpents lay eggs' is a separate clause.
rationale: Reproductive mode and litter size are recorded for snakes in the Reptile Database and in the amniote life-history compilation. Those fields can confirm internal egg retention with live birth in Vipera and can show that live birth is not confined to vipers. The 'about twenty' and 'all in one day' details are only as complete as the species-level litter data, which is enough to test the claim and not enough to make every clause equally sharp.
